newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Dollar gush seen easing Brazil devaluation fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gush seen easing Brazil devaluation fears.

text.p: A gush of dollars are flowing into Brazil, boosting reserves to record highs and allaying fears raised last month of an imminent currency devaluation, economists and fund managers said.
"It is ironic that we are seeing such high reserves when a lot of people were looking at Brazil in terms of devaluation," said Carlos Kawall, Citibank's chief economist in Brazil.
"It is important to see that there are no signs of a loss of confidence," Kawall said.

Despite panic selling in local stocks last month - which sent Latin American bourses plunging on rumors Brazil would follow Asian countries along the devaluation path - Brazil is drawing a flood of dollars.

The central bank this week said hard currency cash reserves in July rose $2.8 billion to a record $59.5 billion. August also promises to deliver a net surplus, with billions of dollars in telecom privatization money and Eurobonds in the pipeline.
Just in the first two working days of August, commercial foreign exchange contracts show a whopping $1.73 billion surplus.
Most of the money is coming in the form of Eurobond and American Depositary Receipt proceeds, short-term speculative capital and cash to pay for recent sales of state assets.
Investors keep a sharp eye on the flows, which are needed to finance Brazil's widening current account balance of payments deficit, expected to hit about $35 billion this year.
Net dollar surpluses also pad foreign reserves, which the government dips into at times to support the strong local currency.
Falling reserves and rapidly expanding current account deficits brought on Mexico's 1994 peso crisis, and more recently, devaluations in Thailand and the Philippines.

Last month's worries about a Brazilian devaluation soon had more or less subsided when Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist Rudiger Dornbusch stoked the fire in a Sunday interview with Folha de Sao Paulo.
"Who's next?" Dornbusch asked after detailing policy shortcomings leading to the Thai devaluation.
Dornbusch, an outspoken critic of Brazil's rigid monetary and foreign exchange policy, said of all Latin American economies Brazil was the most likely to face a currency crisis.

Brazil's current account deficit of about 4.5 percent of gross domestic product - while not nearly as high as Thailand's and Mexico's before their problems - was worrying, especially with a currency overvalued, according to Dornbusch, by at least 25 percent.
Dornbusch's prescription was a 15 percent to 20 percent devaluation of the currency prior to the 1998 presidential election - a move seen extremely unlikely by local investors and economists.
"We don't see a devaluation of this kind until after the election unless there is a strong external shock," Citibank's Kawall said.
Investors note that they will keep their eye on net captial flows, which serve as a good early warning signal.

Fabio Rodrigues de Oliveira, a fund manager at BankBoston Brazil who oversees $4.8 billion in local assets, noted: "Last month there was nervousness in the stock market but currency and debt traders never panicked because they saw the dollars coming in."

While net dollar inflows should remain strong through August, a recent Reuter survey of eight Brazilian banks and research firms forecasts net cash reserves falling to $57.3 billion by the end of the year.
